findings.text: The first paragraph says plainly what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, so a newcomer can explain it after one paragraph.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: A link to the next steps sits in the header, so a newcomer does not have to scroll through the whole study to find out how to start.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: prerequisites, a clone command, a setup script and a one-line first request. The page does not say which operating systems are supported, or that running Claude Code needs an account and may cost money.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm" ... "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page title and heading name a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena lands on a study of someone else's tool and has to read the lede to see why.

The page's demonstration is a study of another project, but Athena's main pitch is turning a request into a traced commit. The page never shows an example of that main output, such as a request, the models used, the cost and the verdict.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: This link in the header is for the repository owner. A newcomer is not an owner and may be confused about whose decisions are meant.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The Counters section refers to transition ids that are only defined in the next section, so a first-time reader meets labels they cannot yet decode.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: This uses Athena's internal terms ("job", "recorded boundary", "edge") without defining them. A newcomer cannot tell what was missing or why it matters.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate, so no failure or retry edge was observed"

findings.text: This refers to a repository folder the newcomer has not seen. It means something to maintainers but tells a first-time visitor nothing.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"

findings.text: Every statement on the page cites a claim, and every claim links to file lines at a pinned commit. This makes the promise of traceability concrete and checkable, which supports the "why it matters" pitch.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."
